content.title: Response to Reviewer pMfG
content.comment:
Q5: How to justify the better performance is coming from robustness rather than representation ability.

A5: We thank the reviewer for pointing this out. We do agree that a better representation on the clean images does provide stronger robustness. To better reflect the model robustness, we propose a new metric to reduce the impact of the model representation on the clean images. Specifically, we take the ratio between the accuracy on the corrupted images and that on the clean images. This metric reflects how much of the accuracy could be preserved when testing on the corrupted images and the accuracy on the clean images are thus normalized. Taking DeViT-B1 as an example, we calculate the ratio of its accuracy on ImageNet-C (54.1%) to the accuracy on ImageNet (79.4%). The result is 68.1%, representing that 68.1% of the accuracy could be preserved. However, the ratio that the accuracy could be preserved for PVTv2 is 65.4%. It is shown that even with comparable accuracy on clean images, DeViT achieves significantly higher performance on the corrupted images and the accuracy retention. This shows that the excellent performance of DeViT in robustness experiments comes from its architectural advantages.

Q6: Typos

A6: Thank you for pointing that out. We have carefully proofread the whole manuscript and fixed these typos in the revision.

content.title: Response to Reviewer pMfG
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the comments. Our responses to the questions are as below.

Q1: The idea is straightforward and shares motivations with others. 

A1: We thank the reviewer for the comments. We would like to highlight that the main insights of our proposed method is the attention factorization/decomposition. The main purpose is to factorize the original NxN attention matrix into several smaller attention matrix with each contains a portion of tokens at different positions. The super-position of the factorized attention matrix are equivalent to the original attention matrix but with the computational complexity changed from O(N^2) to MO(K^2) with M denotes the number of groups we have divided and K denotes the window size. Thus, converting the computational complexity to be within local windows. Although our proposed network architecture is not complicated in terms of engineering implementation, it is well motivated and shows significant improvement with the same computational complexity compared to window-based methods when with detailed apples to apples comparison. The detailed design choices of such implementations are also well motivated as below:

(1) The first choice is to keep the same number of patches for self-attention calculation as the Swin window, but the kept patches should represent a larger area. This practice is based on our observation that the local windows lose global modeling capability and gives suboptimal representation within the preferred local area. The drawback of this practice is amplified when noises are injected. We hence verified this on ImageNet-C and observed that Swin transformer suffers a larger accuracy drop. We thus propose to take the same number of patches as the Swin transformer but from a larger area. The dilation is one of the implementations that could serve our purpose.

(2) We want to introduce multi-scale information for the attention calculation. The group of the attention heads again is a way of implementation of our proposed insights. Since the main motivation is to increase the attended area, another common practice is to downsample the feature map such that each token has a larger receptive field. However, directly downsampling all tokens will lead to severe loss of information and thus degrade the accuracy. We thus propose to downsample the feature maps at multiple scales such that the original information is preserved (for the attention heads with no downsampling) while the attended area is also enlarged to enable the modeling of long-range dependency for self-attention calculation.

Q2: Comparision to related works. 

A2: We thank the reviewer for recommending these related works. In response, we have added corresponding analysis and comparisons of these methods in Sec.2 of the revision.

Q3: Mobile setting in Table 2?

A3: We thank the reviewer for the comments. We realize that the training of the networks under mobile setting is special and need extra training design. We thus only compare with PVTv2 which has the same training recipe as our models.  However, we do agree that the mobile setting is an important direction, and we will keep it as a future work. 

Q4: List comparisons for Throughput. 

A4: We thank the reviewer for pointing this out. We strongly agree with your comments and have supplemented the relevant results in Figure 5. We compare our DeViT with PVTv2. The complexity of PVTv2 is O(N^2)/SR, which in essence is still quadratic with the image size. In contrast, the complexity of DeViT is M O(K^2) where the local window size K is much smaller than the image size. Therefore, as shown in Figure 5, the FLOPs of DeViT grows linearly with the image size. The efficiency advantage of our DeViT becomes more pronounced as the size increases, and the comparison results with PVTv2 in Figure 5 prove this conclusion.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a novel defactorization self-attention mechanism (DeSA) that enjoys both the advantages of local window cost and long-range dependency modeling. DeSA includes three steps: i) defactorization, evenly divide the entire feature map into a series of local windows; ii) dilated sampling, uniformly sample a fixed number K points in each local window; iii) cross-window fusion, fuse the features of the sampled points at the same position in different windows. To obtain fine-grained details in the obtained key tokens, the method introduces mixed-grained multi-head attention by gradually enlarging the local window size in different heads. After all, compared with Swin-T, our DeViT-B2 significantly improves classification accuracy by 1% and robustness by 6%, and reduces model parameters by 14%.

content.title: Response to Review UYJk
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the comments. Our responses to the questions are as below.

Q1: The proposed method sounds like leveraging dilated sampling to construct global representations for long range information. This is a little bit similar to the global representations in "ETC: Encoding Long and Structured Inputs in Transformers" or "Set Transformer: A Framework for Attention-based Permutation-Invariant Neural Networks"

A1: Thank you for the comments. In response, we have discussed and cited the above reference in Sec 2 of the revision. These articles are indeed excellent, but our DeViT is still different from them. Specifically, DeViT differs from ETC in two aspects: i) DeViT can build local and global dependencies simultaneously without feeding two independent sequences; ii) ETC uses the radius to limit the L2L range, which is equivalent to the local window with dilation rate 1 used in DeViT. In contrast, DeViT applies local windows with different dilation rates simultaneously through multiple attention groups. DeViT also differs from Set Transformer in two aspects: i) DeViT uses local windows with dilation rate to reduce computational complexity, it is significantly different from the way Set gets a low-dimensional matrix I; ii) Set Transformer is suitable for processing order-independent set data, which is quite different from image processing.

Q2: Miss some stronger baselines, such as "Focal Attention for Long-Range Interactions in Vision Transformers"

A2: Thank you for the constructive suggestions. The Focal Attention is in indeed a strong baseline model. But our DeViT still has better performance and we have supplemented the relevant results in Table 2 of the revision. Specifically, our DeViT achieves similar classification accuracy but with a 14% reduction in model size.

This paper requires thorough editing.   Some words are made up or used to mean the exact opposite of their actual definition (see below).  I was not sure of what I was reading most of the time.  The math looks incorrect in places, the dimensions do not line up.

Specifics:
+ "Defactorize" is not a word, and it does not make any sense as used by the authors.  In mathematics, factorization or factoring consists of writing a number as a product of several factors, usually smaller or simpler objects of the same kind.  Thus, to "defactorize" means to perform the multiplication and return the original whole number.  However, the authors define the word "defactorize" to mean " evenly divide the entire feature map into a series of local windows".  This does not make sense.

This does not make sense. If one "mitigates global dependency" with a local window, then this is an advantage and not a drawback   The authors are misusing the word "mitigate".  Systems that employ local or global dependencies have their own specific shortcomings. Both local and global windows impact robustness, but in different ways.

content.title: Response to Reviewer CMFC
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the comments. Our responses to the questions are as below. 

Q1: Miss some valuable references

A1: Thanks to the reviewer for recommending these missing key references. In response, we have added these key references in the revision (Section 2). 

Q2: "Defactorize" is not a word, and it does not make any sense as used by the authors. In mathematics, factorization or factoring consists of writing a number as a product of several factors, usually smaller or simpler objects of the same kind. Thus, to "defactorize" means to perform the multiplication and return the original whole number. However, the authors define the word "defactorize" to mean " evenly divide the entire feature map into a series of local windows". This does not make sense.

A2：Thank you for pointing this out. In response, we have renamed our proposed model as factorization vision transformer (FaViT) in the revision. 

Q3: This does not make sense. If one "mitigates global dependency" with a local window, then this is an advantage and not a drawback The authors are misusing the word "mitigate". Systems that employ local or global dependencies have their own specific shortcomings. Both local and global windows impact robustness, but in different ways.

A3: Thanks for the constructive suggestions. Through in-depth analysis of the indicated work, we find that its definition of global dependency is different from that in our work. In the indicated work, the global dependency is defined as the perceived overall information of the vision. However, in our work the global dependency is defined as the relationship of one token to all the other tokens in the image. In addition, we agree that using both global and local features is more important, which is also demonstrated by our experimental results in Figure 8. We have revised the writing to make our description more accurate in the revision.

Q4: Incorrect symbols and formulas.

A4: Sorry for the typos and mistakes. In response, we have carefully proofread the entire manuscript and corrected them in the revision. 

Q5: What does some parameters mean? What are their dimensions? What does Q, K and V mean? What are their sizes?

A5: Thank you for pointing these issues out. We have added more clarifications to make the meanings and dimensions of these symbols more clear in the revision (Section 3.1).

content.title: Response to Reviewer D6N5
content.comment:
$ \textbf{You have obviously misunderstood our work} $. Our DeViT aims to achieve high performance and robustness with computational complexity linearly with respect to the image resolution.

Q1: In my opinion, the proposed dilated sampling mechanism is also essentially a pyramid structure. Therefore, the author should at least discuss their differences with these pyramid structure-based transformers.

A1: We thank the reviewer for the comment but would like to point out that $ \textbf{our proposed DeViT is not a pyramid structured } $ $ \textbf{ architecture} $. Essentially, DeViT’s computational complexity is O(N), theoretically lower than that of pyramid-based architectures O(N^2). In fact, DeViT enjoys the computational complexity quadratically proportional to the window size and hence should be naturally categorized into window-based architectures. As already shown in Figure 5, the computational complexity of DeViT grows linearly with the increase of image resolution, while the pyramid models grow quadratically. We have clearly described such difference in Sec. 3.2. Specifically, DeViT assigns different dilation rates to distinct head groups to obtain multiple local windows with the same spatial size but varying sampling range. Since the self-attention is computed within each local window, the complexity of DeViT is hence quadratic with the window size and linear with the image resolution. 

Q2: I think that the criticism is not reasonable because Swin is capable of modeling long dependency with shifted-window-based self-attention beyond local-window-based self-attention.

A2: We thank the reviewer for the comment. However, again, $ \textbf{there is a deviation in your understanding of Swin Transformer} $. The point we are claiming, as described in Sec. 3.1, is that the window-based self-attention mechanism models only short-range dependencies within a local window. The Shift operation in Swin does increase the range of dependency modeling but not with self-attention based algorithm. The long-range dependency is modelled via some overlapping tokens in consecutive Swin transformer blocks and this method is not as strong as the direct global self-attention mechanism. To intuitively show the difference, we visualized the generated attention maps by Swin transformer in Figure 6(c). Swin transformer demonstrates clear local window effect and is hence weak in modeling long-range dependency.

Q3: What is the difference between the multi-head self-attention (components of standard transformer block) and the proposed head grouping?

A3: We have clearly presented this point in Sec.3.2. $ \textbf{DeViT and multi-headed self-attention are completely different} $. As shown in Figure 3, we assign different dilation rates for distinct groups. Therefore, there exist large differences in the way that each head group extracts features. In addition, different head groups have different learning goals, i.e., to extract features at different granularities. While for traditional multi-head self-attention, the feature extraction methods and the roles of different head groups are the same.

Q4: What is the advantage of the proposed method? The complexity of the proposed method seems to be the same as Swin if we set N to m^2 in Eq. 13.

A4: $ \textbf{Our advantage is to achieve higher performance and robustness with} $ $ \textbf{linear computational complexity} $. Therefore, it is true that our DeViT has the same computational complexity as Swin Transformer, which has been clearly stated in Sec.3.2. As shown in Figure 5, DeViT’s computational complexity is linear to the image resolution. Table 2 shows that DeViT significantly outperforms Swin in terms of accuracy. Meanwhile, Table 6 shows that DeViT enjoys much stronger robustness than Swin. In addition, Figures 4 and 6 visualize the attention maps generated by DeViT and Swin, respectively, which demonstrate the clear superiority of our DeViT.

Q5: The performance improvements are also limited when we compare it with the existing PVTv2-B0.

A5: We would like to highlight that our proposed DeSA has improved theoretical computational complexity from O(N^2) to O(N). As the input image size becomes larger, our DeSA reduces the complexity by two times compared to PVTv2, with comparable number of parameters. $ \textbf{Our strengths focus on computational complexity and robustness} $. As shown in Figure 5, PVTv2 is twice as computationally complex as DeViT at a resolution of 1120. In robustness experiments, DeViT demonstrates much stronger robustness than PVTv2 with the same model size.

Q6: What is the N set to in Eq. 13？

A6: We have defined it in Equation 7 of Sec 3.2. It represents the number of points sampled in each local window.

My main concerns weren't well addressed after carefully reading the responses from authors and comments from other reviewers. Therefore, I **still keep my original score as Reject because of limited novelty and insufficient discussions or comparisons**. I don't think (**very confidently**) that I misunderstand their work.

- **Limited Novelty**. 
    - First, the Swin-Transformer is the first time to achieve the computational complexity of O(N). The proposed DeviT also obtains the same computational complexity as Swin-Transformer. Furthermore, the authors claim that one of the main advantages is efficiency. However, the proposed DeviT has approximate (even higher) Flops when compared to existing PVTv2 (e.g. FaViT-B3 with 8.5G vs. PVTv2-B3 with 6.9G in Table 2, FaViT-B0 with 24.6G vs. PVTv2-B0 with 25.0G in Table 4.) 
   - Second, most recent works attempt to model long-dependency with low computation costs as pointed out by other two reviewers (UYJk and pMfG). However, the authors didn't discuss and compare them. 
   - Third, the authors use the existing techniques (i.e., dilated convolution) for modeling long-range dependency with the computational complexity of O(N). 

   Overall, I don't find any new contributions to the community.

- I want to **further correct the concept of pyramid structure and understanding of Swin-Transformer**. 

   - First, the pyramid structure has been widely used in various vision tasks and it may be implemented by multiple structures such as Spatial Matching (SM) schemes for image recognition, Feature Pyramid Network (FPN) for object detection, and Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling (ASPP) for semantic segmentation but shared a similar spirit (e.g., using features in multiple granularities). The proposed key FaSA module (as shown in Fig. 1c) is the same as the ASPP (Fig 4) in DeepLab [1]. So, I think the proposed FaSA is also a pyramid structure. 
   
   - Second, the long-dependency ability is indeed boosted by shift-window and patch merging in Swin-Transformer, and shift-window is also elegantly implemented by masked self-attention. 

      Here, I directly copy the original descriptions in the Swin-Transfomer paper as follows: 
      - "To produce a hierarchical representation, the number of tokens is reduced by patch merging layers as the network gets deeper. "
      - "The window-based self-attention module lacks connections across windows, which limits its modeling power. To introduce cross-window connections while maintaining the efficient computation of non-overlapping windows, we propose a shifted window partitioning approach which alternates between two partitioning configurations in consecutive Swin-Transformer blocks."
      - "The shift-window introduces connections between neighboring non-overlapping windows and the **self-attention** computation in the new windows crosses the boundaries of the previous windows."

         For more details, please refer to Sec. 3.2 (Shifted Window based Self-Attention) in Swin-Transformer paper.
 
- In addition, I would like to remind the authors to carefully read my question before answering. For example:
   - What is the difference between the multi-head self-attention (components of standard transformer block) and the proposed head grouping? The authors answer the difference between DeViT and multi-head self-attention. 
   - The performance improvements are also limited when we compare the proposed method with the existing PVTv2-B0. The authors answer the theoretical computational complexity of the proposed method.
   

[1] Deeplab: Semantic image segmentation with deep convolutional nets, atrous convolution, and fully connected crfs, TPAMI 2017.

content.title: Response to Reviewer D6N5 (II)
content.comment:
Q6: Whether the proposed FaSA should belong to a pyramid structure.

A6: We have to highlight that $\textbf{ the reviewer is trying to confuse the concepts of “pyramid”}$. In the initial review, the reviewer categorize all transformer architectures into two board category: window based transformer(represented by Swin) and Pyramid based transformer(represented by PVT) and the reviewers have also given corresponding citations so that we confirm our understanding on this is correct. Under such context, the reviewers categorize our method into pyramid based transformer and this is obviously wrong as our proposed FaSA enjoys a local window computational cost. Please refer to our previous response A1 and Sec. 3.2 for details.

Q7: Whether the Swin could model long-range dependency.

A7: Thanks for your comment. We have to highlight that our claim is that the Swin transformer do not model the long-range dependency within a single attention block. This practice could have some negative effects as we have proven in our paper in Table 5 where the robustness is 7% lower and clean acc is also 1% lower. Here, we directly copy the original description in Swin-Transformer paper [1]:
“The shifted window partitioning approach introduces connections between neighboring non-overlapping windows in the previous layer and is found to be effective in image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation, as shown in Table 4.”
For more details, please refer to the official code of Swin transformer [2]. $\textbf{The Shift operation is only performed between multiple blocks}$. As shown Figure 4 in original Swin-Transformer paper [1], only adjacent local windows perform information interaction. When several blocks are connected in series, the range of dependency can be expanded by multiple Shift operations. However, in our FaViT, each FaSA block could model mixed-gained long-range dependency.

[1] Swin Transformer: Hierarchical vision transformer using shifted windows, ICCV 2021.
[2] https://github.com/microsoft/Swin-Transformer

content.title: Response to Reviewer D6N5 (I)
content.comment:
Thanks for your comments again, however we have to point out the misunderstandings on several points as detailed below.

Q1: (1) First, the Swin-Transformer is the first time to achieve the computational complexity of O(N). The proposed DeviT also obtains the same computational complexity as Swin-Transformer.  (2) Third, the authors use the existing techniques (i.e., dilated convolution) for modeling long-range dependency with the computational complexity of O(N).

A1: We would like to highlight again that our main contribution is to achieve significantly higher accuracy with same computational complexity as Swin. $\textbf{The understanding on our contribution as}$ $\textbf{achieving window computational complexity is wrong}$. The main novelty is the attention factorization where we factorize the conventional attention matrix into several sub-attention matrix such that the super-position of the sub-attention matrix can better approximate the original full attention matrix. The dilation operation is simply a way of implementing our proposed algorithm. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to factorize attention matrix to achieve global attention calculation with local computation cost. In order to help reviewers understand clearly, we upload the schematic in the anonymous github repository (https://github.com/anonymous0519/DeViT). The improvements are also verified to be significant. For an example, on ImageNet C, our proposed FaViT-B2 achieves 82.1% accuracy which surpasses Swin-T counterpart by a large margin of 1% while significantly reducing the parameters by 14%. And our FaViT-B2 also improves detection accuracy 3% in Table 3, segmentation mIoU 4% in Table 4. Furthermore, our FaViT-B2 shows astounding model robustness in Tab 4, whose robustness accuracy retention significantly improves 7% compared with Swin-T.

Q2: Furthermore, the authors claim that one of the main advantages is efficiency. However, the proposed DeviT has approximate (even higher) Flops when compared to existing PVTv2 (e.g. FaViT-B3 with 8.5G vs. PVTv2-B3 with 6.9G in Table 2, FaViT-B0 with 24.6G vs. PVTv2-B0 with 25.0G in Table 4.)

A2: Thanks for your comment. One of the goals of our proposed FaViT is to find a trade-off between long-range modeling capability and computational cost. Concretely, we hope to achieve a computational complexity of O(N) while retaining high performance and robustness. As a result, $\textbf{the proposed FaViT achieves this goal and the efficiency advantage becomes more }$ $\textbf{pronounced as the image size increases}$. As shown in Figure 5, we compare the throughputs (imgs/s) between PVTv2-B2 and FaViT-B2. It is obvious that our FaViT is more efficient and the superiority is highlighted when the input image is large.

Q3: Second, most recent works attempt to model long-dependency with low computation costs as pointed out by other two reviewers (UYJk and pMfG). However, the authors didn't discuss and compare them.

A3: Thanks for your comment again, but we have explained it in the responses to the two reviewers mentioned above, and discussed and compared these models in the reversion Sec 2 and Table 2.

Q4: What is the difference between the multi-head self-attention (components of standard transformer block) and the proposed head grouping? The authors answer the difference between DeViT and multi-head self-attention.

A4: Thanks for your comment. The differences between the multi-head self-attention and our proposed attention are $\textbf{different in terms of both}$ $\textbf{input, way of implementation}$. For MHSA, input are the feature tokens with each tokens share the same receptive. Differently, our proposed attention force each head to have different size of receptive field to model the factorization effects. Please refer to figure 1 in the paper and our previous response for details.

Q5: The performance improvements are also limited when we compare the proposed method with the existing PVTv2-B0. The authors answer the theoretical computational complexity of the proposed method.

A5: $\textbf{We would like to highlight that a fair comparison with our proposed method should be }$ $\textbf{Swin transformer since the}$ $\textbf{computational complexity are the same}$. PVTv2 has a quadratic complexity so that the computational cost becomes huge as the input-resolutions become large as shown in Fig. 5 in the paper. $\textbf{However, even with PVTv2, the advantages are still obvious.}$ Compared with PVTv2-B0, Table 2 shows that the proposed FaViT-B0 has a smaller model size, similar FLOPs, but a 1% improvement in classification accuracy, which is considered as significant on large dataset such as ImageNet. Table 3 and Table 4 show that FaViT-B0 has similar performance at a smaller model size. Table 5 and Table 6 show that FaViT-B0 significantly improves the robustness under smaller model size.
